# Tesakuṇajātaka (Ja 521)

**ID:** Ja 521
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Tesakuṇajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Tesakuṇajātaka* (Ja 521), titled *Three Birds* in English, is a birth story set at Jetavana, where the Buddha admonishes the King of Kosala on righteous statecraft (*dhammena rajjaṁ kāretabbaṁ*) [Emmanuel 2013; Fausböll 1891]. The Master warns the king that royal misconduct corrupts officials and leads to suffering, contrasting the misery of sensual indulgence with the blessings of abstaining from evil courses [Emmanuel 2013]. To illustrate royal virtue, the Buddha narrates a past life in which King Brahmadatta of Benares, being without a son, adopted three eggs from a nest in his royal park—an owl, a myna bird (*sālikā*), and a parrot—rearing them as royal foster children under the names Vessantara, Kuṇḍalinī, and Jambuka [Winternitz 1933; Migot 1954]. When grown, the three exceptionally wise birds instruct the king in *rājadharma* (the duties and ethical conduct of a ruler) [Winternitz 1933]. At the story's conclusion, the Bodhisatta is identified as the parrot Jambuka, with the other birds identified with Sāriputta, Uppalavaṇṇā, and Ānanda [Fausböll 1891; Migot 1954].

The text serves as an important source for early Buddhist political philosophy [Emmanuel 2013; Tambiah 1976]. The birds counsel the monarch to eliminate wrath, arrogance, and falsehood, to judge equitably, govern justly, protect subjects from violence, and restrain the senses [Moore 2016; Emmanuel 2013]. It asserts that divine fortune (Lakṣmī) favors bold, benevolent, and virtuous sovereigns rather than capricious or oppressive rulers [Shaw 2006]. The discourse also articulates the doctrine of the five royal strengths (*balāni*) underpinning legitimate kingship: physical strength of arms (*bāhabalaṁ*), material wealth (*bhogabalaṁ*), counsel of ministers (*amaccabalaṁ*), high birth (*abhijaccabalaṁ*), and intellectual wisdom (*paññābalaṁ*), which is esteemed as the greatest among them [Tambiah 1976].

**Sources**

- [Emmanuel 2013] Steven M. Emmanuel, A Companion to Buddhist Philosophy (2013) — Discusses early Buddhist political ideas on the duties and powers of a king and quotes verses on avoiding anger and deceit.
- [Fausböll 1891] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka Together with Its Commentary, Vol. 5 (1891) — Supplies Pali text incipit, Kosala setting, and the identification of previous births (*samodhāna*).
- [Jones 1949] J. J. Jones, The Mahāvastu, Vol. I (1949) — Notes the close correspondence between Jātaka 521 and the Mahāvastu tale of the childless king.
- [Migot 1954] André Migot, 'Un grand disciple du Buddha: Sāriputra' (1954) — Details the three bird species, their foster names, and their identification with Sāriputta, Uppalavaṇṇā, and the Bodhisatta.
- [Moore 2016] Matthew J. Moore, Buddhism and Political Theory (2016) — Details the moral and governmental counsel given by the three birds to King Brahmadatta.
- [Shaw 2006] Miranda Shaw, Buddhist Goddesses of India (2006) — Discusses the Tesakuṇa Jātaka's ethical treatment of Lakṣmī's blessings on a righteous and energetic ruler.
- [Tambiah 1976] S. J. Tambiah, World Conqueror and World Renouncer (1976) — Details the five royal powers (*balāni*) of kingship formulated in the Tesakuṇa Jātaka.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, A History of Indian Literature, Vol. II (1933) — Summarizes the narrative of childless King Brahmadatta and the three birds instructing him in rājadharma.
